title: Exclusive: Verde Technologies Will Test Perovskite Solar Cells on the ISS in 2027
html:
Solar cell manufacturer Verde Technologies signed a contract to send its lightweight, ultra-thin perovskite solar cells to the ISS NET June, company officials told Payload.

The mission—part of NASA’s Materials International Space Station Experiment (MISSE) , which focuses on testing new materials and components on the orbital lab—will involve bolting Verde’s solar cells to the outside of the ISS for six months before they’re returned to Earth for analysis.

The research aims to validate Verde’s perovskite solar cell technology in space for the first time and open the door for Verde to begin producing and selling solar cells to spacecraft operators at scale.

“The plan for us is to validate the technology completely, then start entering the market in steps,” CEO Jean-Noel Poirier told Payload. “Starting with satellites [and] high-altitude drones that actually really value that type of material…then smallsats and big sats, constellations [and orbital] data centers.”

Pressing need: Verde was founded to serve the terrestrial solar energy market. Its ISS mission will come just one year after the company pivoted to focus on space and high-altitude applications.

The company’s goal is to lighten the solar-cell load for satellites and drones, reducing the overall weight of the vehicles, and—for the space market—driving down total mission cost. A massive increase in demand from satellite builders also drove the pivot, according to Verde officials.

The space industry is projecting tens of thousands of new satellites in orbit over the next five years, many of which are focused on higher-energy applications, such as power beaming, and orbital data centers. The result is that the total demand for satellite solar panels is growing even faster than the demand for spacecraft.

Unfortunately for satellite builders, there aren’t many options out there for lightweight solar cells.

“You have two solutions: One is gallium arsenide, which is the cells used by NASA for long-term exploration. They work great…but there is no [production] capacity,” Poirier said. “Two, you have silicon. Silicon is plentiful on Earth…but it is not a good solution for space. It degrades…it’s inefficient…It’s heavy, it’s clunky, and the transparent elephant in the room right now is that [most] silicon comes from China.”

New kid on the block: Verde’s plan is to offer a third option to the market. Unlike other solar cell manufacturers, who print perovskite onto silicon or glass, Verde is commercializing a perovskite-only cell, printed onto a lightweight, flexible substrate. With this method, the company’s solar cells can be folded or rolled tightly during launch, then deployed into extra-large structures—with the help of partners to maintain the total array’s rigidity.

And without using silicon, the company can get around any international supply-chain headaches, and directly serve the US defense market.

“The industry needs American-made or European-made—let’s say non-Chinese dependent solutions—that work great in space, at low cost, at scale, etc. And that’s what we do,” Poirier said.

Correction: This story was updated to correct who Verde signed a deal with for the ISS mission. It was a contractor.
summary: Solar cell manufacturer Verde Technologies signed a contract to send its lightweight, ultra-thin perovskite solar cells to the ISS.
